subsection: 2. A Peripheral European Region: the Mezzogiorno

notes.b: The Mezzogiorno is the Mediterranean, peripheral region you can study as a contrast to the core Paris Basin. It is southern Italy and its islands, which together form the peripheral south of the country.
points: It is made up of eight regions: Abruzzo, Molise, Campania, Puglia (Apulia), Basilicata, Calabria, Sicily and Sardinia. This is why the region is described as the South and its islands, not one single area.
The name Mezzogiorno means midday, a reference to the strong midday sun of the south.
It covers about 40% of Italy's area but holds only about one-third of its population: about 20 million people (2020s), out of an Italian population of about 59 million (2024).
Rome and the region of Lazio lie north of the Mezzogiorno and are not part of it, so never include them when you describe the region.
Sicily and Sardinia are autonomous regions with a special statute (their own legal status), which gives their regional governments extra powers. This reflects their separate island identity.
notes.tip: The Mezzogiorno is southern Italy and its islands only. Do not include Rome or Lazio.

notes.b: Peripheral means far from the economic core, where the main markets, industry and wealth are. Distance, relief (the shape and height of the land), history and politics combine to keep the South behind the North.
points: Distance: the South is far from the EU's core markets and from the industrial North of Italy, which raises the cost of moving goods.
Relief and climate: the land is mostly mountainous or hilly and summers are dry, which limits farming, transport and settlement.

History: the South, formerly the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, became part of a united Italy in 1861, and the North–South gap widened after unification. Land stayed in large estates, which kept farming backward.
Organised crime and emigration drain investment and people from the South, so the region loses both money and workers.

The North–South divide is known as the questione meridionale (the southern question). The Mezzogiorno produces only about 22% of Italy's GDP (the value of all goods and services made), and its GDP per head is a little over half that of the Centre-North (recent years).
Unemployment in the South is roughly two to three times the North's rate (recent years).
Contrast: the Paris Basin, studied in region s1, is a core European region; the Mezzogiorno is the peripheral counterpart.
notes.tip: When a question asks for two contrasting European regions, make the contrast explicit: core Paris Basin against peripheral Mezzogiorno. Do not repeat Paris Basin facts here.

notes.b: You may be asked to draw an outline map of a European region and mark named features. These are the Mezzogiorno features you can draw and name.
points: Rivers: the Volturno in Campania, the longest river of the southern mainland; the Ofanto in Puglia; the Basento in Basilicata.
Urban centres: Naples, Bari, Taranto, Brindisi, Palermo, Catania and Reggio Calabria.
Relief: the Apennines (the mountain chain down the peninsula), the Sila in Calabria, Mount Etna and Vesuvius.
Lowlands: the Tavoliere di Puglia around Foggia, the Campanian plain and the plain of Catania.
Agricultural and industrial areas: the Tavoliere (durum wheat) and the Bari–Brindisi–Taranto industrial triangle, which is the South's own industrial area.
notes.tip: A sketch map question asks for a named river, two urban centres, a named relief feature and a named agricultural or industrial area. Pick one of each from this list.

notes.b: The climate has hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters, with rain concentrated in the cooler months. This pattern drives the region's water problems and its farming.
points: Summers are hot and dry because the subtropical high-pressure belt (a zone of sinking, dry air) moves north over the region.
Lowland summer (July) averages around 25°C or more. This heat is why summers need irrigation.
Winters are mild and wet, with rain brought by Atlantic depressions (low-pressure weather systems); most rain falls between October and March.
Coastal winter (January) averages about 9–12°C.
Annual rainfall is under 600 mm on parts of the Puglia lowlands and Sicily, but much higher on the Apennines. This is why irrigation is needed on the lowlands, while the high Apennines are wetter.
The sirocco is a hot, dry, dusty wind from the Sahara that adds to the dryness of summer.
Summer drought causes water shortage, while intense autumn and winter downpours cause flash floods (sudden floods after heavy rain).
Farmers respond with irrigation (supplying water to crops) and drought-tolerant crops.
notes.tip: For questions on the impact of climate on primary activity, link the dry summer to irrigation and drought-tolerant crops.

notes.b: Mountains and hills cover most of the region, and the lowlands are small and mostly coastal. This shapes where people farm and live.
points: The Apennines run the length of the peninsula, forming its spine.
The highest point of the Apennines is Corno Grande (Gran Sasso, Abruzzo), at 2,912 m. This is why the interior is so hard to farm or cross.
The Calabrian uplands are dominated by high ground, including the Sila plateau. Because the high ground leaves little flat land, farming and settlement are limited.
The Tavoliere di Puglia, around Foggia, is the largest plain of peninsular southern Italy. Because it is flat, it suits large-scale farming, such as durum wheat.
The Campanian plain around Naples and the plain of Catania, Sicily's largest plain, are the other main lowlands.
Mount Etna in Sicily, about 3,300 m, is Europe's highest active volcano. This is why the island has both a volcanic hazard and fertile volcanic soil.
Steep slopes limit farming, transport and settlement to small areas and push villages onto hilltops.
notes.tip: Say the land is mostly mountainous or hilly. Do not give a percentage of upland.

notes.b: The region is geologically restless, so earthquakes and volcanoes are part of life in the South. Here are the local examples; they are also a source of fertile soil.
points: The region lies where the African and Eurasian plates meet, which is why it has earthquakes and volcanoes.
Messina and Reggio Calabria were destroyed by the earthquake and tsunami of 28 December 1908, with tens of thousands killed.
Irpinia, Campania, 23 November 1980: thousands killed.
L'Aquila, Abruzzo, 6 April 2009: magnitude 6.3, about 300 deaths.
Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 79 and last erupted in 1944. Because it is still active, it remains a hazard to nearby Naples.
Etna and Stromboli are active volcanoes. This is another sign of the plate boundary beneath the region.
Campi Flegrei is a volcanic caldera (a large crater formed by collapse) west of Naples, where the ground rises and falls, called bradyseism, around Pozzuoli.
notes.tip: For Messina 1908 and Irpinia 1980, give only 'tens of thousands' and 'thousands' killed. Sources disagree on exact tolls.

notes.b: Soils vary sharply with bedrock (the solid rock under the soil) and slope, and this decides which land can be farmed well.
points: Thin, stony soils cover much of the upland, where the bedrock is close to the surface. This is why upland farming is poor.
Terra rossa is red clay soil that forms on limestone, for example in Puglia.
Fertile volcanic soils on Vesuvius and Etna, in Campania and Sicily, support vineyards and orchards.
Alluvial soils (soils deposited by rivers) on the lowlands are used for intensive farming. Because rivers deposit fresh fertile material, these soils suit intensive farming.
Calanchi are gullied badland slopes on clay, for example in Basilicata. Because clay erodes easily in heavy rain, it forms gullies, so the land is of little farming use.
Soil erosion is worsened by deforestation, overgrazing and the winter downpours that wash bare soil away.
Sarno, Campania, 5–6 May 1998: saturated volcanic ash slid as mudflows, killing about 160 people.

notes.b: Rivers follow the climate: they carry water in the wet winter and shrink in the dry summer. This makes them poor sources of water and transport.
points: Rivers are short and steep, so they flood quickly after rain.
Winter: heavy rain turns the rivers into torrents. This is why rivers flood so quickly.
Summer: many channels run dry. This is why rivers cannot supply irrigation water in the season crops need it most.
Fiumare are wide, dry, stony riverbeds in Calabria and Sicily that flood after heavy rain.
Few rivers are navigable (deep and steady enough for boats), so they are of little use for transport.
The Apulian Aqueduct (Acquedotto Pugliese), built in the early 20th century, carries water from the Sele river springs in Campania across the Apennines to Puglia, which has little water of its own.

notes.b: Before reform, most land was held in large estates, which kept productivity (output per worker or hectare) low.
points: Latifundia are large estates owned by absentee landlords, who lived away from them.
The latifundia were worked by landless day labourers (braccianti) paid wages.
The main uses of the estates were extensive wheat growing (low output per hectare) and sheep grazing.
Small hill farms were fragmented into scattered plots, which were hard to farm efficiently. So the farmers could not use their land efficiently.
Productivity was low on both the estates and the small hill farms.

notes.h: Land reform and the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno
notes.b: After the Second World War the state tried to fix the old estate system and develop the South. It did this through land reform and a development fund.
points: Land reform laws of 1950 expropriated (took by law) parts of the large estates and gave plots to peasants.
The Cassa per il Mezzogiorno (Fund for the South) ran from 1950 to 1984. Its aim was to develop the South with state money.
Its work included land reclamation (making wet or unusable land farmable), drainage, irrigation dams, aqueducts and roads. These works improved land and water supply for farming.
It built new settlements on reclaimed lowlands for the new smallholders (small farm owners).
Malaria was eradicated from the lowlands after the Second World War, which made them safe to settle.
From the late 1950s the Cassa also funded industry.

notes.b: Modern farming in the South is specialised: it grows Mediterranean crops suited to the climate and soils, often for markets beyond the region.
points: Durum wheat is grown on the Tavoliere di Puglia around Foggia, Italy's main durum wheat area, for pasta. The dry summers and flat land suit it.
Puglia is Italy's leading olive-oil region. Olives are drought-tolerant, so they suit the dry climate.
Sicilian blood oranges are grown on the plain of Catania near Etna.
Lemons are grown on the Amalfi coast and around Sorrento. These crops are specialised and sold beyond the region.
Irrigated market gardening (growing vegetables for sale) on the Campanian plain includes San Marzano tomatoes grown near Vesuvius.
Puglia and Sicily are major wine producers. Vines are drought-tolerant, so they suit the dry summers.
Specialised Mediterranean produce is grown for markets, and agri-food firms (food-processing businesses) process it.
notes.tip: For development of agriculture, link each crop to relief, climate and markets.

notes.b: Despite reform, southern farming faces natural, economic and social problems.
points: Drought and water shortage reduce yields where land is not irrigated. This is why irrigation matters.
Soil erosion removes topsoil from the hills. Steep slopes and winter downpours make this worse.
Xylella fastidiosa, a bacterial disease of olive trees, was detected in the Salento (southern Puglia) in 2013 and has killed millions of olive trees.
Ageing farmers and rural depopulation leave fewer people to work the farms. This is why farms are harder to keep going.
Caporalato is illegal gangmaster hiring and exploitation of farm labourers, many of them migrants. This is why farm work can be unsafe and underpaid.
Many farms depend on EU Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) support (payments to farmers), so they are exposed if it changes.

notes.b: Forests were cut down in the past, and the dry climate still threatens what remains.
points: Historic deforestation of the Apennines has left slopes exposed to erosion. Without tree roots to hold the soil, rain washes it away.
Reafforestation (replanting trees) of the Sila plateau in Calabria was carried out under the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno.
Summer wildfires destroy woodland in the dry season. The dry heat makes fires spread easily.

notes.b: Fishing in the South is based on Mediterranean ports such as Mazara del Vallo in Sicily, and overfishing now limits catches.
points: Mazara del Vallo, Sicily, is one of Italy's main fishing ports.
Traditional tuna trapping, the mattanza, took place in Sicily at Favignana; it has now largely ended.
Overfishing (catching fish faster than stocks recover) in the Mediterranean reduces catches.

notes.b: The South has some energy resources and is also a landing point for imported gas, with growing renewable power.
points: The Val d'Agri oilfield in Basilicata is Italy's largest onshore oilfield and one of the largest onshore oilfields in western Europe. This makes Basilicata a significant energy source.
Gas pipelines from Algeria land at Mazara del Vallo, and gas from Libya lands at Gela, both in Sicily.
The Trans Adriatic Pipeline (TAP), carrying gas from Azerbaijan, lands in Puglia and began flowing in 2020.
Puglia and Sicily are among Italy's leading regions for wind and solar power, which suit their sunny, open land.

notes.b: Industry in the South has stayed weak compared with the North. Several causes reinforce each other.
points: Distance from markets raises the cost of transporting goods to buyers. This is why firms in the South struggle to compete.
Poor infrastructure: weak roads, railways and ports make transport slow and costly. This is why firms find it costly to move goods.
Small local market and low incomes: local demand is too small to support many firms.
Lack of capital and enterprise: few local firms have the funds or entrepreneurs to start up.
Organised crime: extortion payments, known as pizzo, deter investment because firms must pay criminals to operate.
Lack of raw materials: few are available locally for heavy industry.
notes.tip: Be ready to give these reasons for weak industry: distance from markets, poor infrastructure, small market, lack of capital, organised crime and lack of raw materials.

notes.h: Growth poles and the industrial triangle
notes.b: The Cassa used state investment to build large growth poles, plants intended to spark industrial growth around them.
points: The Taranto steelworks was built by the state firm Italsider in the 1960s; it became one of Europe's largest steelworks, later called Ilva and now Acciaierie d'Italia.

Petrochemical plants (making chemicals from oil and gas) were built at Brindisi and at the Priolo–Augusta complex near Siracusa in Sicily, and a refinery at Gela in Sicily. These plants were state-led, part of the growth-pole policy.
The Bari–Brindisi–Taranto triangle is the South's own industrial area, not the industrial triangle of the North.
Cathedrals in the desert is the name for large, capital-intensive (needing huge investment but few workers) state plants that created few jobs and few local spin-off firms.
notes.tip: Keep the two triangles apart. Milan–Turin–Genoa is northern Italy, the contrast; the South's triangle is Bari–Brindisi–Taranto.

notes.b: Car plants were another attempt to bring large-scale manufacturing to the South.
points: The Alfasud plant at Pomigliano d'Arco near Naples opened in 1972 and now builds the Fiat Panda. It brought car making close to Naples, a large city with workers.
Fiat's Melfi plant in Basilicata opened in the early 1990s and is now part of Stellantis. It brought a major car plant to inland Basilicata.
Fiat's plant at Termini Imerese, Sicily, closed in 2011. The closure shows how fragile southern manufacturing jobs are.
notes.tip: Fiat's Turin plants are in northern Italy, not the Mezzogiorno.

notes.b: Some of the South's industry has brought serious problems as well as jobs.
points: In 2012 a court ordered parts of the Taranto steelworks seized because of pollution linked to illness in Taranto.
Lavoro nero is undeclared work in the informal, or black, economy, outside tax and labour rules, so workers lack protection and the state loses tax.

notes.b: Current policy tries to close the North–South gap using EU and Italian funds and new growth sectors.
points: For EU cohesion policy (EU funding to reduce regional inequality) 2021–27, most of the South, including Campania, Puglia, Basilicata, Calabria and Sicily, is classed as less developed regions, with GDP per head below 75% of the EU average.
A single Special Economic Zone for the South (ZES Unica) began in January 2024, offering tax credits and simplified permits.
Italy's post-Covid National Recovery and Resilience Plan reserves at least 40% of its territorially allocated funds for the South.
Aerospace is a growth sector: Leonardo builds Boeing 787 fuselage sections at Grottaglie, near Taranto. This shows the South moving beyond heavy industry.
Agri-food is also a growth sector, building on the region's specialised produce. This is because local produce can be processed locally for added value.

notes.b: Exams ask you to explain secondary activity (manufacturing) using factors such as labour and markets. For each factor, give the fact and the challenge it creates in the Mezzogiorno.
points: Labour: there is a large pool of unemployed workers, but low incomes limit local spending.
Raw materials: heavy industry depends on inputs brought in from outside, such as gas by pipeline.
Markets: the small local market and distant European markets mean firms face high transport costs.
Infrastructure: slow motorway upgrading and limited high-speed rail make transport costly and slow.
Government policy: the Cassa's growth poles and the ZES Unica attract investment, but capital-intensive plants create few jobs.
notes.tip: Questions ask for development of secondary activity with reference to two factors: labour, transport, raw materials, markets, infrastructure or government policy. Give the challenge each factor creates.

notes.b: Tourism is a tertiary (service) activity that suits the South's sun, scenery and history.
points: Visitors come for the climate, the coast, the volcanoes of Vesuvius and Etna, the heritage sites and the food.

UNESCO sites (World Heritage Sites): Pompeii and Herculaneum (1997); the Amalfi Coast (1997); the Valley of the Temples, Agrigento (1997); the trulli of Alberobello, Puglia (1996); the sassi of Matera (1993); the historic centre of Naples (1995).
Taormina, Sicily, is a coastal tourist town. It is a coastal town, so it draws visitors for the sea and scenery.
The Costa Smeralda in north-east Sardinia was developed as a luxury resort from the 1960s by the Aga Khan. This was planned luxury tourism, so it differs from the mass tourism elsewhere.
Agriturismo is farm-stay tourism, bringing visitors into the countryside. This is why it suits the countryside, such as farms in hill areas.
notes.tip: Use named sites only and no invented tourist totals or percentages.

notes.b: Tourism brings benefits, but it also creates problems.
points: Seasonality: most visitors come in the summer months, leaving tourist jobs short-term. This is why tourism gives uneven year-round income.
Coastal overdevelopment: abusivismo, illegal building including on coasts, damages the landscape.
Crime: organised crime can affect businesses and tourist areas.
Poor transport: slow road and rail links limit access to the South's attractions.

notes.b: Transport links open markets and bring investors and tourists, so poor links keep the region remote. The region's remoteness is partly a transport problem.
points: The Autostrada del Sole (A1, Milan–Rome–Naples) was completed in 1964. It linked the South to the industrial North, which opened routes for goods and people.
The A2 Salerno–Reggio Calabria motorway has been notorious for decades of slow, costly upgrading. This slow progress is why it counts as a transport problem.
High-speed rail reaches Naples and Salerno; the Naples–Bari line is being upgraded.
Gioia Tauro, Calabria, is Italy's largest container transhipment port (where containers are moved between ships). Because ships transfer cargo there, it is a hub for sea trade.
Ferries cross the Strait of Messina between Villa San Giovanni/Reggio Calabria and Messina. They link Sicily to the mainland, so island goods and visitors can move.
Ferries sail from Bari and Brindisi to Greece and Albania. This is why these ports matter for trade with Greece and Albania.
A bridge across the Strait of Messina has been proposed, approved and challenged repeatedly over many years, so do not assume it is built.
notes.tip: Do not state the Messina bridge is built, under construction or cancelled. Questions ask about the importance of transport to economic development in two contrasting regions.

notes.b: Services provide jobs in the South, but not the same kind as in the North.
points: Public-sector employment (jobs paid by the state) is a large source of jobs in the South. This is because private industry is weak.
Informal employment, such as lavoro nero (undeclared work), is also large.
Private services are weaker than in the North.

notes.b: Population is concentrated on the coastal lowlands and in cities, and thins out in the interior.
points: Campania has about 400 people per km², one of Italy's most densely populated regions. This is because of its fertile volcanic lowlands and the city of Naples.
Basilicata has about 55 people per km² and only about 540,000 people (2020s). This is because it is largely mountainous and remote.
Dense coastal lowlands and cities contrast with sparse interior uplands.
Fertile volcanic lowlands attract settlement; thin, stony soils and dry uplands do not.
Cities offer jobs in services and industry, drawing people from the interior.
notes.tip: Questions ask for population distribution throughout a region. Contrast Campania with Basilicata and give reasons such as relief, water, soils and jobs.

notes.b: Poverty and lack of jobs have pushed people out of the South for well over a century.
points: Large-scale emigration from the late 19th century went to the USA and Argentina. People left because of poverty and lack of work.
After the Second World War, emigration went to the industrial cities of northern Italy (Turin, Milan) and to Germany, Switzerland and Belgium.
Out-migration continues, as young graduates leave the region for work elsewhere in Italy and abroad. This is because jobs in the South are limited.

notes.b: Fewer births and continued departures mean the population is ageing, while some migrants arrive across the sea.
points: Fertility (births per woman) was once high but is now very low: Italy's rate is about 1.2 children per woman (2023), among the lowest in the EU. This is why the population is ageing.
Sardinia's fertility rate is among the lowest in Italy.
Inland villages are ageing and depopulating, with few young residents. This is because young people leave and few children are born.
€1 house schemes in depopulating villages, for example Sambuca di Sicilia, sell houses for €1 to attract new residents.
Lampedusa, an Italian island south of Sicily, is a main landing point for migrants crossing the Mediterranean. It lies south of Sicily, so it is close to the sea route from Africa.

notes.b: Standard Italian is shared across the country, but the South also has strong dialects and minority languages.
points: Standard Italian is the official language.
Strong regional dialects include Neapolitan and Sicilian.
Arbëreshë is spoken by Albanian-speaking communities in Calabria and Sicily, settled from the 15th century. This is why Albanian is still spoken there.
Griko is a Greek dialect spoken in the Salento (Puglia) and southern Calabria.
Sardinian is spoken in Sardinia.
Catalan is spoken in Alghero, Sardinia.

notes.b: Religion remains an important part of southern life.
points: The population is mainly Roman Catholic, with strong traditional practice.
The Feast of San Gennaro, patron saint of Naples, includes the ritual of the liquefaction of his blood.

notes.b: Culture in the South combines folk traditions, regional identity and football. Religion and language, covered above, are part of it too.
points: The tarantella is a fast folk dance of southern Italy, named after Taranto.
Neapolitan song includes 'O sole mio'.
SSC Napoli won Serie A (Italy's top football league) in 1987, 1990, 2023 and 2025.
The art of the Neapolitan pizza maker was added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2017.
Sicily and Sardinia are autonomous regions with a special statute, giving their regional governments extra powers.
Clientelism, the exchange of votes for favours, and organised crime both influence local politics.
notes.tip: For the culture of a region, cover religion, language, politics, music and dance, and sport.

notes.b: Naples is the South's largest city. Its rapid, unplanned growth left serious problems.
points: Naples is the South's largest city, with about 900,000 people in the city and about 3 million in the metropolitan city (2020s).
Palermo has about 630,000 people (2020s).
The Spanish Quarter (Quartieri Spagnoli) is a dense, overcrowded historic district. Overcrowding there followed rapid growth.
The Vele di Scampia are large 1960s–70s public housing blocks on the northern edge of Naples, linked with Camorra (Naples organised crime) drug dealing; several have been demolished.
The Naples waste crisis of 2007–08 left rubbish piled in the streets after landfills filled. This shows how rapid growth overwhelmed city services.
The Camorra was involved in illegal dumping and burning of waste in the Terra dei Fuochi (land of fires), between Naples and Caserta. This is why the area is called the land of fires.
Rapid, unplanned growth fed by rural migration produced overcrowding and illegal building.

notes.h: Factors in the growth of Naples
notes.b: Several advantages explain why Naples grew into the South's largest city.
points: Site: the city lies on the Bay of Naples beside Vesuvius.
Port: the harbour gave access to sea trade. Trade through the port helped the city grow.
Capital: Naples was the capital of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies until 1861, a centre of government.
Fertile volcanic hinterland (the surrounding area) supports farming and markets around the city.
Rural in-migration: people moved from the countryside to the city for work and services.
notes.tip: Questions ask for the factors in the growth of one urban area: use site, port, capital, hinterland and in-migration.

notes.b: Rural settlement reflects the region's history of danger and poverty, and today many villages are emptying.
points: Hilltop villages were built for defence and to avoid the malarial coastal lowlands. This is why many villages sit high up and far from the farmland.
Matera's sassi (cave dwellings) were evacuated in the 1950s, and their residents moved to new housing; the sassi became a UNESCO site in 1993.
Matera was European Capital of Culture in 2019. This shows how a once-evacuated town was revived as a cultural attraction.
Depopulation and abandonment of interior villages continue as young people leave.

Gullied badland slopes on clay, e.g. in Basilicata.
Wide, dry, stony riverbeds in Calabria and Sicily that flood after heavy rain.
The slow rising and falling of the ground, as at Campi Flegrei around Pozzuoli.
A bacterial disease of olive trees, detected in the Salento in 2013.
Illegal gangmaster hiring and exploitation of farm labourers, many of them migrants.
Farm-stay tourism.
Illegal building, including on coasts.
Undeclared work in the informal economy.
Albanian-speaking communities in Calabria and Sicily, settled from the 15th century.

factCards.term: The Mezzogiorno: its eight regions and its share of Italy
factCards.definition: Abruzzo, Molise, Campania, Puglia, Basilicata, Calabria, Sicily and Sardinia (not Rome or Lazio). About 40% of Italy's area and about a third of its people: about 20 million of 59 million. 'Mezzogiorno' means midday.

factCards.term: Why the Mezzogiorno is a peripheral region
factCards.definition: Far from the EU core and northern Italian markets; mountainous land and dry summers; history (joined united Italy in 1861, with land held in large estates); organised crime; emigration. It makes about 22% of Italy's GDP; unemployment is two to three times the North's.

factCards.term: Sketch map of the Mezzogiorno: features to name
factCards.definition: Rivers: Volturno (Campania), Ofanto (Puglia), Basento (Basilicata). Cities: Naples, Bari, Taranto, Palermo, Catania. Relief: the Apennines, the Sila, Etna, Vesuvius; the Tavoliere lowland. Areas: the Tavoliere (durum wheat); the Bari–Brindisi–Taranto industrial triangle.

factCards.term: Mezzogiorno climate: causes and figures
factCards.definition: Hot, dry summers as subtropical high pressure moves north (July 25°C or more); mild, wet winters from Atlantic depressions (January 9–12°C), most rain October–March. Under 600 mm on parts of Puglia and Sicily, more on the Apennines. Sirocco: hot, dusty wind from the Sahara.

factCards.term: Impact of climate on primary activity in the Mezzogiorno
factCards.definition: Summer drought causes water shortage, so farmers grow drought-tolerant olives, vines and durum wheat and irrigate citrus; winter downpours cause flash floods and soil erosion; summer wildfires destroy woodland. The Apulian Aqueduct carries water to dry Puglia.

factCards.term: Relief of the Mezzogiorno and its effects on people
factCards.definition: The Apennines form the spine (Corno Grande, 2,912 m), with the Calabrian uplands and the Sila; lowlands are small and coastal: the Tavoliere di Puglia, the Campanian plain, the plain of Catania. Steep slopes limit farming and transport and push villages onto hilltops.

factCards.term: Earthquakes and volcanoes in the Mezzogiorno: named examples
factCards.definition: Where the African and Eurasian plates meet. Earthquakes: Messina (28 December 1908, tens of thousands killed), Irpinia (1980), L'Aquila (2009, magnitude 6.3). Volcanoes: Vesuvius (AD 79; last erupted 1944), Etna (about 3,300 m), Stromboli; Campi Flegrei near Naples.

factCards.term: Soils of the Mezzogiorno: types and problems
factCards.definition: Thin, stony upland soils; terra rossa on limestone (Puglia); fertile volcanic soils on Vesuvius and Etna; alluvial lowland soils. Problems: erosion from deforestation, overgrazing and downpours (calanchi in Basilicata); Sarno mudflows (1998, about 160 killed).

factCards.term: Traditional farming in the Mezzogiorno and the 1950 land reform
factCards.definition: Latifundia of absentee landlords, worked by braccianti, grew wheat extensively and grazed sheep; hill farms were small and fragmented; productivity was low. Land reform laws in 1950 took parts of the large estates and gave plots to peasants.

factCards.term: Cassa per il Mezzogiorno: what it did for the land
factCards.definition: The Fund for the South (1950–1984) paid for land reclamation, drainage, irrigation dams, aqueducts and roads, and new farmhouses and villages on lowlands made safe once malaria was eradicated; it reafforested the Sila. From the late 1950s it also funded industry.

factCards.term: Modern agriculture in the Mezzogiorno: crops and where they grow
factCards.definition: Durum wheat for pasta on the Tavoliere around Foggia; olive oil in Puglia, Italy's leading region; blood oranges on the plain of Catania; lemons on the Amalfi coast and around Sorrento; San Marzano tomatoes near Vesuvius; wine in Puglia and Sicily.

factCards.term: Problems facing agriculture in the Mezzogiorno
factCards.definition: Drought and water shortage; soil erosion; Xylella fastidiosa, found in the Salento in 2013, has killed millions of olive trees; ageing farmers and rural depopulation; caporalato, the exploitation of migrant farm workers; dependence on CAP support.

factCards.term: Why industry is weak in the Mezzogiorno
factCards.definition: Distance from markets; poor roads, railways and ports; a small local market with low incomes; little capital or enterprise; organised crime demanding extortion (pizzo); few raw materials.

factCards.term: Growth poles in the Mezzogiorno: named examples and criticism
factCards.definition: State plants backed by the Cassa: the Taranto steelworks (Italsider, 1960s), one of Europe's largest; petrochemicals at Brindisi and Priolo–Augusta (Sicily); a refinery at Gela; the Bari–Brindisi–Taranto triangle. 'Cathedrals in the desert': few jobs or spin-offs.

factCards.term: Car and aerospace plants in the Mezzogiorno
factCards.definition: Alfasud at Pomigliano d'Arco near Naples (1972), now building the Fiat Panda; Fiat's Melfi plant, Basilicata (early 1990s, now Stellantis); Fiat's Termini Imerese plant, Sicily, closed in 2011. Leonardo builds Boeing 787 fuselage sections at Grottaglie, near Taranto.

factCards.term: Problems for Mezzogiorno industry: pollution, crime, black economy
factCards.definition: In 2012 a court seized parts of the Taranto steelworks over pollution linked to illness; Cosa Nostra, the 'Ndrangheta, the Camorra and Sacra Corona Unita demand pizzo, deterring investment; lavoro nero (undeclared work) is widespread.

factCards.term: Recent policy to develop the Mezzogiorno
factCards.definition: Most of the South is an EU 'less developed region' for 2021–27; the single Special Economic Zone for the South (ZES Unica) began in January 2024 with tax credits and simpler permits; Italy's post-Covid recovery plan reserves at least 40% of allocated funds for the South.

factCards.term: Tourism in the Mezzogiorno: attractions and problems
factCards.definition: Climate, coast, volcanoes and food; UNESCO sites: Pompeii and Herculaneum, the Amalfi Coast, Agrigento's Valley of the Temples (all 1997), Alberobello's trulli (1996), Matera's sassi (1993). Problems: seasonality, abusivismo on coasts, crime, slow transport.

factCards.term: Transport in the Mezzogiorno and its importance
factCards.definition: Autostrada del Sole (A1, Milan–Naples, 1964); decades of slow upgrading on the A2 to Reggio Calabria; high-speed rail only to Naples and Salerno; Gioia Tauro, Italy's largest transhipment port; ferries to Sicily, Greece and Albania. Poor links keep the region remote.

factCards.term: Population distribution in the Mezzogiorno, with reasons
factCards.definition: Dense coastal lowlands and cities: Campania has about 400 people per km². Sparse interior uplands: Basilicata has about 55 per km² and only about 540,000 people. Fertile volcanic lowlands, water and city jobs attract people; thin soils and steep, dry uplands do not.

factCards.term: Emigration from the Mezzogiorno: when and where
factCards.definition: From the late 19th century to the USA and Argentina; after the Second World War to Turin and Milan and to Germany, Switzerland and Belgium; today young graduates still leave for northern Italy and abroad.

factCards.term: Fertility, ageing and immigration in the Mezzogiorno
factCards.definition: Italy's fertility is about 1.2 children per woman (2023), Sardinia's among the lowest; inland villages age and empty, some selling €1 houses (Sambuca di Sicilia); Lampedusa, south of Sicily, is a main landing point for migrants crossing the Mediterranean.

factCards.term: Culture of the Mezzogiorno: language, religion, music and sport
factCards.definition: Neapolitan and Sicilian dialects; Arbëreshë, Griko, Sardinian and Catalan (Alghero) minorities; strong Catholic practice, as at the Feast of San Gennaro, Naples; the tarantella; 'O sole mio'; SSC Napoli (Serie A 2023, 2025); Neapolitan pizza (UNESCO 2017).

factCards.term: Factors in the growth of Naples
factCards.definition: A site on the Bay of Naples beside Vesuvius; a port for sea trade; capital of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies until 1861; a fertile volcanic hinterland; rural in-migration. About 900,000 people in the city and about 3 million in the metropolitan city.

factCards.term: Urban problems of Naples
factCards.definition: Overcrowding in the Spanish Quarter; the Vele di Scampia estates, linked to Camorra drug dealing (several demolished); the 2007–08 waste crisis; illegal dumping and burning in the Terra dei Fuochi; unplanned growth and illegal building.

factCards.term: Rural settlement and development in the Mezzogiorno
factCards.definition: Hilltop villages were built for defence and to escape malarial lowlands; land-reform farmhouses dot the plains; Matera's sassi were evacuated in the 1950s, became a UNESCO site (1993), and Matera was European Capital of Culture (2019); interior villages are emptying.

questions.prompt: Examine the impact of climate on the development of primary economic activities in a peripheral European region that you have studied.
questions.model: The region is the Mezzogiorno. Summers are hot and dry because the subtropical high-pressure belt moves north, so summer drought causes water shortage; lowland July averages are around 25°C or more. Most rain falls between October and March, brought by Atlantic depressions, and annual rainfall is under 600 mm on parts of the Puglia lowlands and Sicily. Farmers depend on irrigation: the Cassa built dams and aqueducts, and the Apulian Aqueduct carries water from the Sele springs across the Apennines to Puglia. Durum wheat is grown on the Tavoliere di Puglia around Foggia, which is suited to the dry conditions; Puglia leads Italy in olive oil; Sicilian citrus, such as blood oranges, is grown on the plain of Catania; and Puglia and Sicily are major wine producers. Irrigated market gardening on the Campanian plain includes San Marzano tomatoes grown near Vesuvius. The sirocco, a hot, dry, dusty wind from the Sahara, adds to summer dryness. Intense winter downpours erode bare hillsides, forming calanchi badlands in Basilicata, and flash floods in the fiumare. Drought, water shortage and erosion together reduce yields on unirrigated land and limit the spread of farming to the small lowlands.

questions.prompt: Account for the development of secondary economic activity in a European region (not in Ireland), with reference to government policy and markets.
questions.model: Secondary development in the Mezzogiorno was driven by state policy rather than by local markets. From the late 1950s the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno funded industry through growth poles: large state-led plants such as the Taranto steelworks, built by Italsider in the 1960s, and petrochemical plants at Brindisi and at Priolo–Augusta near Siracusa. These are part of the Bari–Brindisi–Taranto industrial triangle. The plants were capital-intensive, so they created few jobs and few local spin-off firms, the cathedrals in the desert. Markets limited growth: the local market is small, incomes are low, and the South is distant from the EU core markets, so transport costs are high. Few local firms could supply the plants, so linkages were weak. Later car plants include the Alfasud plant at Pomigliano d'Arco near Naples, opened in 1972 and now building the Fiat Panda, and Fiat's Melfi plant in Basilicata, opened in the early 1990s. Fiat closed its Termini Imerese plant in Sicily in 2011, showing how dependent the region is on firms that can leave. EU cohesion funding classes most of the South as less developed regions, and the ZES Unica from January 2024 offers tax credits and simplified permits. Organised crime, through extortion payments, deters investment. State policy therefore created pockets of heavy industry but not self-sustaining growth.

questions.prompt: (i) Name one tertiary activity in a European region (not in Ireland). (ii) Explain the advantages this region has for it. (iii) Describe one challenge it faces.
questions.model: (i) Tourism in the Mezzogiorno. (ii) Advantages: the Mediterranean climate gives hot, dry summers suited to coastal holidays; the coastline includes the Costa Smeralda in north-east Sardinia, developed as a luxury resort from the 1960s; volcanoes such as Vesuvius, Etna and Campi Flegrei attract visitors; and the region has many UNESCO sites, including Pompeii and Herculaneum (1997), the Amalfi Coast (1997), the Valley of the Temples at Agrigento (1997), the trulli of Alberobello (1996), the sassi of Matera (1993) and the historic centre of Naples (1995). Food and farm-stay tourism add to the attraction, including the Neapolitan pizza maker's art, on UNESCO's list since 2017, and agriturismo. (iii) Challenge: poor transport. The A2 Salerno–Reggio Calabria motorway has been notorious for decades of slow, costly upgrading, and high-speed rail reaches only Naples and Salerno. Slow links limit access to the South's attractions, and the region's remoteness is partly a transport problem.
